name: text/vtt
description:
WebVTT (Web Video Text Tracks) is the W3C caption and subtitle format that the HTML `track` element loads. A file is plain UTF-8 text: the word `WEBVTT`, then cues giving a start time, an end time and the text to show between them.

Beyond captions it carries chapters, descriptions and arbitrary metadata cues. Cue settings can position text anywhere in the frame rather than only along the bottom. That range is why it displaced SubRip, the `.srt` format, on the web, even though SubRip files are simpler to write.

furtherReading.title: W3C WebVTT: The Web Video Text Tracks Format

name: application/manifest+json
description:
A web app manifest is the JSON document that tells a browser how to install a site as an application. It gives the name, icons, start URL, display mode and theme colour. The W3C Web Application Manifest specification defines it, and a page points at one with a `link` element whose `rel` is `manifest`.

It is what makes a Progressive Web App installable rather than merely bookmarkable. The registered extension is `.webmanifest`, though a great many sites serve the same document as `manifest.json`.

name: application/ld+json
description:
JSON-LD is JSON carrying a `@context` that maps its keys onto IRIs, so a document that reads like ordinary JSON also has machine-readable meaning. The W3C specifies it.

Most of the structured data on the web is JSON-LD. It appears inside a `script` element carrying this media type, describing a page's schema.org entities to search engines. Because the context does the linking, code that ignores it entirely still sees plain, readable JSON.

name: text/cache-manifest
description:
An application cache manifest listed the files a browser should retain for offline use. It arrived with HTML5 as AppCache, and both the W3C and browser vendors have since removed it.

It failed for a specific reason worth remembering. A manifest that could not be fetched left users stuck with stale files, and the update model gave a page no way to recover. Service workers replaced it. Files still exist in old projects, so the type is worth recognising, but nothing new should use it.

name: application/dash+xml
description:
An MPD (Media Presentation Description) is the manifest for MPEG-DASH, standardised as ISO/IEC 23009-1. It is an XML document listing the periods of a presentation, the adaptation sets within each, and the representations a player may choose between. For every segment it gives the URL or the byte range.

DASH is codec-agnostic, and the MPD is where that shows. A player reads it and switches representation as available bandwidth changes, and the format itself does not care what codec is inside.

name: text/wgsl
description:
WGSL (WebGPU Shading Language) is the shader language for WebGPU, specified by the W3C GPU for the Web working group. WebGPU accepts WGSL source directly rather than a compiled bytecode, so a `.wgsl` file is human-readable text that the browser compiles.

It exists because the web needed a shading language it could parse and validate itself. The browser then translates it safely to Direct3D, Metal and Vulkan, without trusting a binary from the page.

name: application/toml
description:
TOML (Tom's Obvious Minimal Language) is a configuration format designed to map unambiguously onto a hash table while staying obvious to read. It has sections in square brackets, `key = value` beneath them, and real types for strings, integers, dates and arrays.

Rust's `Cargo.toml` and Python's `pyproject.toml` are where most people first see it. Against YAML it trades expressiveness for predictability, since there is far less that can be written two different ways.

name: application/cbor
description:
CBOR (Concise Binary Object Representation) is a binary format defined by RFC 8949. It covers roughly JSON's data model and adds byte strings, unambiguous integers and floats, and an extension mechanism through numeric tags.

It is designed to be encoded and decoded without a schema and in very little code. That is why it appears in constrained devices, in CBOR Object Signing and Encryption (COSE), and in WebAuthn attestation.

name: application/geo+json
description:
GeoJSON encodes geographic features as JSON, defined by RFC 7946. A document is a Feature or a FeatureCollection, and each feature pairs a geometry (Point, LineString, Polygon, or their multi- forms) with arbitrary properties.

RFC 7946 fixed the coordinate reference system as the World Geodetic System 1984 datum, WGS 84, with longitude before latitude. That single decision removed the largest source of disagreement between implementations of the earlier community specification.

name: application/json-patch+json
description:
JSON Patch describes a change to a JSON document, defined by RFC 6902. A patch is an array of operations. Each names one of add, remove, replace, move, copy or test, and points at a location with a JSON Pointer.

Sent as the body of an HTTP PATCH it lets a client alter one field without transmitting or overwriting the whole resource. The `test` operation is what makes an update safely conditional. If the document is not in the expected state the patch fails, rather than overwriting a concurrent edit without warning.

name: application/node
description:
This type labels JavaScript intended to run as a Node.js CommonJS module rather than to be delivered to a browser. The registration is maintained by the Node.js Technical Steering Committee.

The registration is candid about the overlap. It notes that the type "occupies the same file extension as other media types". It also says a `.js` file "should be considered ambiguous if the intended execution environment is unknown". Server-side and browser JavaScript share the extension, and a web server should still send [text/javascript](/text/javascript).

name: application/sql
description:
RFC 6922 registers this type so that a file of SQL statements can be labelled as such in transit. The registration says nothing about which dialect the statements are written in.

That silence matters. A dump from PostgreSQL, from MySQL and from SQLite all carry this same type, and none of them will load into the others unedited. The type tells you the file is SQL, not that your database can read it. The unregistered spelling still in common use is [application/x-sql](/application/x-sql).

name: application/x-sql
description:
This is the unregistered form of the SQL media type, and the one tools are more likely to send. It was in use before RFC 6922 registered [application/sql](/application/sql), and carried on afterwards, as `x-` types generally do.

Neither form replaces the other. Tools emit whichever they were written against. Both mean the same thing: a file of SQL statements whose dialect is not stated anywhere in the label.

furtherReading.title: Let's Solve the File Format Problem!

name: application/zstd
description:
Zstandard is a lossless compression format defined by RFC 8878. At its default setting it reaches roughly gzip's ratio several times faster, and at high settings it compresses considerably harder than gzip can.

Its distinguishing feature is the trained dictionary. Give it a sample of the small documents you mean to compress, and it derives a dictionary from them. Each document then compresses well despite being far too small for the algorithm to find redundancy in on its own.

furtherReading.title: RFC 8878 - Zstandard Compression and the 'application/zstd' Media Type

name: application/sarif+json
description:
SARIF (Static Analysis Results Interchange Format) is the OASIS standard for reporting what a code analysis tool found. A run records the tool and the rules it applied. It also records every result, with its location, severity and enough surrounding context to be understood without rerunning the tool.

It exists so that every linter and scanner stops inventing its own output format. GitHub code scanning consumes SARIF, which is most of why analysis tools now emit it alongside whatever they produced before.

name: application/spdx+json
description:
SPDX (Software Package Data Exchange) is the Linux Foundation's standard for describing what a software release contains. It covers the packages, their versions and licences, and the relationships between them. This type is the JSON serialisation of an SPDX document.

It is one of the formats accepted as a software bill of materials. That is what moved SPDX from a licence-compliance tool into something shipped alongside releases and checked by procurement.

name: application/vnd.mermaid
description:
Mermaid diagrams are written as plain text and rendered to SVG. A flowchart or sequence diagram is therefore stored in version control and reviewed as a diff, rather than as an opaque attachment that has to be opened.

The syntax is line-oriented: name the diagram type, then declare nodes and the edges between them. Built-in rendering in GitHub and GitLab markdown is why it spread beyond its own tooling.

name: application/vnd.apache.parquet
description:
Parquet is the Apache Software Foundation's columnar storage format. Values from a single column are stored together. A query touching three columns out of two hundred therefore reads only those three, and each column compresses well because everything in it is alike.

A file also carries its own schema and per-column statistics, letting a reader skip entire row groups that cannot satisfy a predicate. That combination is why it became the default for analytical data at rest. Where Parquet optimises storage, [application/vnd.apache.arrow.file](/application/vnd.apache.arrow.file) optimises passing data between processes.

name: application/vnd.apache.arrow.file
description:
Arrow's IPC (inter-process communication) file format writes a columnar table to disk. A footer holds the schema and the position of every record batch, so a reader can seek directly to any batch instead of scanning from the start.

The point is Arrow's in-memory layout. Because the file holds the same representation the library already uses in memory, reading is closer to mapping than to parsing. The form without a footer, for pipes and sockets, is [application/vnd.apache.arrow.stream](/application/vnd.apache.arrow.stream).

name: application/vnd.apache.arrow.stream
description:
This is the streaming form of Arrow's IPC (inter-process communication) format. It is a schema message followed by record batches, written and read strictly in order, with no footer at the end.

Having no footer means there is nothing to seek to, so a consumer cannot jump to the tenth batch. It also means the stream does not have to exist in full before reading starts. That is what makes this the right choice over a socket or a pipe, where the random access of [application/vnd.apache.arrow.file](/application/vnd.apache.arrow.file) was never available anyway.

name: text/vcard
description:
vCard is the contact format defined by RFC 6350, which specifies version 4.0. A card is a run of properties such as `FN`, `TEL`, `EMAIL` and `ADR`, between `BEGIN:VCARD` and `END:VCARD` lines. One file may hold many cards in sequence.

It is what an address book exports and what a phone attaches when someone shares a contact. The registration lists both extensions, but `.vcf` is the one almost every implementation writes.

name: text/xml
description:
RFC 7303 registers `text/xml` alongside `application/xml` for XML documents. The two are functionally equivalent, and the RFC recommends [application/xml](/application/xml) for general use.

The distinction is historical. A `text/` type once implied the content was readable without special tooling. The two types also differed in how a missing charset parameter was interpreted. RFC 7303 settled that: both now default the same way, leaving little reason to prefer this spelling beyond the many servers already sending it.

name: application/vnd.api+json
description:
JSON:API is a convention for building JSON APIs. It fixes how resources, relationships, pagination, filtering, sparse field selection and errors are shaped, so those decisions stop being renegotiated on every project.

The media type is part of the specification rather than incidental to it. A server signals JSON:API semantics by sending this type, and a client asks for them by content negotiation on it. That is why the type matters more here than for most JSON formats.

name: text/x-opml
description:
OPML (Outline Processor Markup Language) is an XML format for nested outlines. Its dominant use by a wide margin is exchanging feed subscription lists. Nearly every feed reader imports and exports OPML, which is what makes moving between readers possible at all.

There is no IANA registration, so the `x-` form is what tools send and expect. The outline structure itself is generic, and a few outliners and mind-mapping tools use it for its original purpose.

furtherReading.title: Let's Solve the File Format Problem!
